title: Applying the Equity Analysis Toolkit to a Realistic Decision
before: A conversation about working through a practice proposal with the Equity Analysis Toolkit, from purpose to an honest recommendation.

turns.text: This course is Applying the Equity Analysis Toolkit to a Realistic Decision. It’s for anyone who reviews service changes, from analysts to supervisors to staff who’ll carry a change out. Rather than talking about equity analysis in general, it walks through one practice proposal from start to finish, beginning with what’s actually being proposed and what it’s meant to achieve.

The proposal would replace several explained information-request routes with one online page, and its purpose is easier organization. The course asks us to separate the change from the promised result. A more organized route for staff doesn’t yet establish easier access or a better experience for people. That gap between purpose and result runs through the whole course.

It’s worth saying the example is invented. DHS publicly describes its intervention and respite redesign as using partner feedback and data to inform proposals, and the course mentions that as context. But the request-route case isn’t part of that redesign or an adopted proposal. The practice questions support reasoning; they don’t replace the current official toolkit or any required analysis.

The first practice question follows the proposal: some people can’t use the page. You’ll decide what the analysis should do. Before that, the course lays out a chain of links, from one online rule to a request that may not reach staff, and asks which link is assumed. That’s a useful habit, because a sequence raises questions without proving a causal chain.

Then comes who encounters the rule. Information, technology, language, format, time, and chosen support can all differ, and saying everyone describes an intention while leaving the task unanswered. The course also asks where each requirement comes from: a legal or policy condition, an operational choice, or a familiar habit. A learner can’t waive a rule, but analysis can show what choice is open.

The evidence section is careful. An account describes experience. A record counts a defined event. A prediction describes something that may happen. Each answers a different question. Missing information isn’t evidence that there’s no barrier, and one account can’t establish the experience of a whole population. I find that framing helps when a team disagrees about what it knows.

The second practice situation moves to the workplace. A supervisor proposes an elaborate application for learning opportunities. It might reveal writing skill, but it might also reward time, guidance, and familiarity with the process. You’ll choose the most useful comparison. The same toolkit questions apply to workplace rules as they do to service rules.

Then the course compares three whole alternatives: the online-only route, an online route with an explained second option, and an assisted conversation. All of them are practice proposals, and all get the same questions about purpose, access, responsibilities, resources, and evidence. You don’t judge one only on convenience and another only on cost.

The third situation is one I think many teams will recognize. A participant says the page leaves no place for a question, and staff add a line saying help is available, but they can’t explain how that help works. You’ll decide what should happen. It’s a good test of when a concern is actually resolved and when it’s only acknowledged.

Near the end, you’ll privately rewrite an impact statement: the online page will improve access for everyone. You’ll state the purpose, the actual proposal, the concern identified, and the evidence still needed, keeping a useful direction without turning it into a promised outcome. A good recommendation lets a reader inspect the reasoning instead of simply accepting a claim.

As you go, think about a proposal in your own work, such as a new form, a channel, a scheduling rule, or an application process. Who is it meant to help, and who might find it harder to use? Bring that situation with you. The toolkit supports your analysis, while decisions stay with the people and processes responsible for them.

guidance.title: Using each kind of evidence well
guidance.text: When a team disagrees, it often helps to sort what each person is relying on. One colleague may be describing what people said, another what the records count, and another what they expect to happen. Each can be valid for its own question. Naming the kind of evidence keeps the conversation focused, and it shows where the honest answer is still unknown.

guidance.title: The same questions at work
guidance.text: Workplace rules also distribute effort and opportunity, from how applications are designed to how learning time is scheduled. Think of one such rule on your team. What is its purpose, who carries the extra effort it creates, and what evidence do you have about its effects? Who would you need to involve before recommending a change?
